items.passage: Mangoes, mostly, though the orchard outside Surabaya had long ago stopped deciding. Arisa counted eleven trees standing and two lying down. Thuy said the fallen ones were resting. Arisa said they were firewood with good manners. They walked the rows the way they had as girls, kicking husks and naming trees after teachers, and Arisa kept her bag on the side away from Thuy. At the gate she took out a parcel: the brass bell Thuy had mailed to her new flat in Jakarta, still in its paper, the knot untouched. Thuy looked at the knot. She did not ask. Arisa said the flat had no window that opened. Then she walked back down the rows, past the teachers, to the eleventh tree, and tied the parcel to its lowest branch, paper and all. They waited for wind. When the bell rang once through the paper, faintly, Thuy reached up and tightened the knot so it would hold through the rains.

Wry and lighthearted toward a walk through a familiar place

items.explanation: 앞부분의 'firewood with good manners' 같은 농담과 건조한 나무 세기가 겉 어조(wry)를 만든다. 중간에 Arisa가 가방을 Thuy 반대편에 두고, 선물을 뜯지 않은 이유로 '열리는 창문이 없다'고 말하는 대목은 선물 거절이 아니라 바람이 닿는 곳에 종을 두려는 배려임을 보여 준다. 끝에서 Thuy가 매듭을 조여 주는 동작이 두 사람의 우정을 이어 가는 따뜻한 속 어조를 완성하므로 A가 정답이다. B는 겉 층만 읽었고, C는 반납을 거절로 읽어 원인을 뒤집었으며, D는 따뜻함의 대상을 과수원 전체로 넓혔다.

items.passage: Three rules for the salt pans, Aoife told every new squad: hats on, water every hour, no running where the crust goes thin. Lanying could recite them backward. She sat on the cooler with her knee strapped, timing sprints with a stopwatch that ran four seconds slow, and called out numbers that made everyone faster than they were. Aoife wrote them down as given. At the break she checked the date on the clipboard twice, then laid it face down on the cooler. The team took the van into town for lunch. Aoife stayed, and after a while walked out past the flags to the place where the white crust had split into plates two years before, and stood there with her whistle cord wound tight around her fingers. Lanying came limping a few minutes later and stood a step behind her. Neither of them said anything about the crust. Aoife handed back the slow stopwatch, and Lanying started it, and they let it run.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?

Brisk and quietly mournful toward a loss the two still carry
Brisk and quietly relieved toward a loss now well behind them

items.passage: By six the kitchen of the boarding house in Manila smelled of garlic rice, and Tyrese was already at the long table with the ledger open. 'Maestro,' he said when Ruoxi came down, and stood, as he did at rehearsals. She waved him back into his chair. The house had been her mother's. For most of a year Ruoxi had left the envelopes from the gas company unopened on the hall shelf, and the stove had gone on lighting every morning. The orchestra paid Tyrese a stipend that rarely lasted the month; on paper his rent was three months owing. Ruoxi poured two coffees and set the sugared one before him. He turned the ledger toward her. Down the margin ran a column of small sums, each dated, each marked with a T: January, February, March. She looked from the column to the hall shelf, where the envelopes no longer were. Then she struck through the line that said his rent was owing and pushed the ledger back. Tyrese closed it and went to wash the pans.
items.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Ruoxi and Tyrese?

items.passage: On Thursdays, after the courts closed, I carried Amelia's proofs down to the press room on Ogarna Street in Gdansk. She was retired by then and wrote small pamphlets about old cases. She called me Clerk, never Dmitri, and I called her Judge; she corrected me once when I forgot. The pressman set her type, and I read it back aloud while she listened with her eyes shut. One week the pamphlet concerned a theft from the harbor office in a winter I remembered, because my father had worked nights there then and had come home at dawn smelling of tar. The draft named no one. At the paragraph about the missing ledger Amelia raised a finger. She took the proof, cut out one line with a ruler and a blade, and counted coins from her own purse for a second setting. The line had given the hour the ledger disappeared: a little after two in the morning. The following Thursday she called me Clerk, as before, and asked me to read more slowly.

items.passage: Four pans hung above the galley stove, and Joaquim's mother had ruled on each before Beatriz came aboard: the big one for beans, the small one for eggs, the copper one for visitors, the black iron one for her alone. Beatriz learned the order in a week. She scrubbed the iron pan when told, oiled it, and hung it on its hook at the far end, handle turned toward the stool where the older woman sat to peel onions. In July the river ran high, and the boat lay docked at Porto Alegre for a month while Joaquim worked the cargo cranes. His mother took her mending up on deck and stayed there. One evening Beatriz, alone below, cooked rice in the iron pan. She left it on the stove afterward, unwashed. From the deck came no word, only the sound of the needle. The next morning the pan was clean and oiled already, hanging not at the far end but on the hook beside the stove, its handle turned toward the spot where Beatriz stood to cook.

The firm rules by which the older woman keeps the bride at arm's length
The place in the household that the older woman is now ready to share
The strained bond between the women that the bride mends by cooking

items.passage: Years later Zaynab could still describe what Consuelo gave her that winter: a tin whistle painted blue, the kind sold to tourists on the quay at Vigo. Consuelo sold fish by day and swept the night pharmacy where Zaynab's mother worked the late counter, and she had once heard Zaynab practicing scales on a school recorder behind the till. The whistle was in the wrong key for every song Zaynab knew. She played it anyway, each night at ten, when the broom came in, and Consuelo leaned on the handle and nodded until the tune was over, sharp notes and all. In March the old woman stopped coming. A nephew took the broom, swept fast, and left. For weeks the whistle stayed in the drawer with the spare receipts. On the last night her mother worked there, Zaynab took it out, wiped it on her sleeve, and stood it upright in the cup of pens beside the register, mouthpiece up, where the next girl behind the counter would reach for a pen and find it.

A mistaken gift that Zaynab plays to spare the old woman's feelings
A friendship that fades once the old woman stops coming to the shop
An imperfect kindness that Zaynab decides to leave for someone new

items.passage: My father kept time by the lamp. At the Colombo station Shamsuddin wound the clockwork that turned the lens every four hours, and he did it with a brass key he had borrowed from the keeper before him and, as far as anyone knew, never given back. When I was eleven I asked why he did not buy one of his own. He said this one fit. At sixteen I refused to learn the winding; I wanted engines, not lamps, and said so loudly, and he wound the clock alone for three more years. When the station was automated, men from the port authority came to collect the key. He handed them a different one from the kitchen drawer, which also fit. On the morning I left for the engineering college in Kandy, he pressed the brass key into my palm and closed my fingers over it. I, Hollis, have kept it on a nail by my own door ever since. When my daughter asks what it opens, I tell her it fits.

items.passage: Soren paid on time. For eleven years he had rented the room above Sunja's net shed at the Jeju harbor, and each month he paid with a handwritten slip that listed every won, down to the coins; once he came back down the stairs to correct a sum he had rounded. In October the winch slipped and crushed a crate of her abalone while he was working it. The harbor office wanted a written account. Sunja offered to write it herself and blame the cable, which was old. Soren thanked her and took the form upstairs. The account he handed her the next morning was ______. Sunja read it on the quay. Beside the cable's age and the crate's weight he had added the minute he looked away to light a cigarette, and she carried the form to the office without changing it.

items.passage: On Sundays Nicolas sold walnut sweets from a folding table outside the cemetery gate in Tbilisi, and on Sundays I, Vesna, bought two and asked for the recipe. He had been a sailor for forty years and answered like a weather report: some sugar, the right walnuts, enough time. I wrote down whatever he said in a notebook. No two lists matched. Last winter he was ill, and the table stood folded against the gate for a month. When he came back, he handed me a paper bag with no sweets in it, only walnuts, a jar of grape must, and a length of string. His instruction was ______. That evening he climbed the four flights to my kitchen, stood at my elbow, and moved my hands until the first strand had set. My notebook stayed shut on the windowsill.

items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Nicolas는 말로 묻는 레시피에 늘 모호하게 답해 왔으므로, 그의 가르침이 말이나 글로 전해질 가능성은 낮다. 빈칸 뒤에서 그는 화자의 부엌까지 올라와 손을 직접 움직여 주며 첫 가닥이 굳을 때까지 곁에 있고, 공책은 닫힌 채로 남는다. 따라서 '말없이 실제로 보여 주는'이라는 C가 두 제약을 모두 만족한다. A는 공책이 닫혀 있다는 사실과 맞지 않고, B는 앞의 습관만 반영해 뒤의 구체적 시범을 설명하지 못하며, D는 지문의 분위기에서 빌린 표현일 뿐 행동의 성격과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: "Hand me the blue pins, if you would," Lakshmi said, and I did, and for an hour we worked the line on the roof of our mother's old boardinghouse in Albuquerque as if no years lay between us. She showed me how to snap a sheet so the wind takes the creases, how to hang shirts by the hem so the shoulders stay smooth, how the adobe parapet holds the morning heat. She had brought me a dozen ironed handkerchiefs, each with my initial stitched in one corner, and I, Jens, thanked her. Between two pillowcases she asked, lightly, whether Mother had still kept her papers in the hall desk. I said that she had. We hung the towels. We hung the dish cloths. I thanked her again for the handkerchiefs. She said they were nothing. That evening I opened the hall desk, took out the deed to the house, and carried it to my room, where I folded one of the handkerchiefs around it and set it under my pillow.

It moves from easy fellowship to guarded courtesy, suggesting the narrator suspects the gift was meant to smooth a question.

items.explanation: 앞부분은 빨래 너는 요령이 촘촘하게 묘사되는 편안한 협동의 장면이다. 서류에 관한 질문 이후 문장이 'We hung the towels.'처럼 짧게 끊기고 감사 인사가 반복되며, 대화의 화제가 사라진다. 저녁에 화자가 집문서를 꺼내 자기 방으로 옮기는 끝 동작은 선물이 그 질문을 부드럽게 하려던 것이 아닌지 의심하게 되었음을 보여 주므로 C가 정답이다. A는 반복된 감사의 겉모습만 읽었고, B는 원인을 화자 자신의 말로 뒤집었으며, D는 조용한 경계를 관계 단절로 지나치게 읽었다.

items.passage: Once a month I brought the supply boat into the cove below the tea terraces, and that spring I found Mio curled behind the fertilizer sacks with a scholarship letter for a college in Plymouth folded in his shoe. He called me Captain Camryn only when he wanted something. I told him he was a nuisance. I told him stowaways ate more than paying cargo, and he proved it, and complained about the diesel smell besides. I set him to scrubbing the deck twice a day. He asked what the fare would have cost. I said more than he had, which was not lying, exactly, only rounding up. On the last run before term I held the boat in the cove an extra hour while he said goodbye to the pickers on the terraces, who had known him since he was small, and I wrote nothing in the log about the extra fuel. When he asked about the fare a third time, I talked about tide tables until he gave up.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Mio as conveyed in the text?
options: Weary impatience with Mio despite brief amusement at his complaints.
Protective care for Mio despite a wish to make amends for a past mistake.
Quiet generosity toward Mio despite a habit of treating him gruffly.
Grudging tolerance of Mio despite calling him a nuisance to the boat.

items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 Mio를 성가신 존재라 부르고 갑판 청소를 시키는 등 퉁명스러운 말투를 보인다. 중간의 'not lying, exactly, only rounding up'은 뱃삯 이야기를 일부러 부풀려 받지 않으려는 망설임을 드러낸다. 뒤에서 화자는 작별 인사를 위해 한 시간을 더 머물고 추가 연료를 기록하지 않으며, 뱃삯 질문을 조수표 이야기로 돌린다. 따라서 거친 말투 아래 조용한 너그러움이 있다는 C가 정답이다. A는 말투만 읽었고, B는 이유를 화자의 과거 죄책감으로 바꾸었으며, D는 지문의 'nuisance'를 빌려 태도를 마지못한 용인으로 낮춰 읽었다.

items.passage:
By seven the gym on Seventy-First smells of floor wax
and the folding chairs are already crooked.
Devon, who rode my father's ferry every summer
and talked the whole way across about nothing,
asks me to the spring dance under the dead scoreboard.
I tell him he dances like a dropped mop.
I tell him I have a shift on the dock,
which is not lying, exactly—
my father would let me off if I asked.
He laughs. He says, Kenya, fair enough,
and goes out whistling through the side door.
I stack the chairs he knocked over
and straighten the ones he didn't,
and when the custodian kills the lights
I stand a while by the bleachers
where he left his jacket, and fold it
sleeve over sleeve, collar up,
and carry it home on the ferry, on my lap,
the whole way across, saying nothing.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Devon as conveyed in the text?

Real fondness for Devon while feeling held back by her duties.
Amused patience for Devon while finding his chatter tiresome.
Guarded fondness for Devon while keeping him at a joking distance.

A는 말투만 읽었고, B는 이유를 의무로 바꾸어 정정 어구와 맞지 않으며, C는 지문의 'talked about nothing'을 빌린 해석이다.

items.passage: Is a delay a kind of confessional? So I wondered at the ferry terminal in Thessaloniki, where weather held the steamer two days and a gentleman named Emre took the bench beside mine. He was bound for a dying friend and could not decide whether to tell him that his son had sold the family vineyard. He decided aloud, hourly, in a fog of cheap tobacco, beginning each round with "Miss Edith, consider." I wrote in my notebook that he talked as a gull walks, much and to no end, and showed the line to the clerk, who laughed. I was not mocking him, exactly, or not only. On the second morning the porter offered me the ladies' waiting room, which was quiet and warm, and I said I preferred the draught. When the steamer was at last called, Emre had still settled nothing, and somewhere between the bench and the gangway the page with the gull on it went into the harbor.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Emre as conveyed in the text?
options: Quiet regard for Emre's struggle despite a mocking account of his manner.
Amused disdain for Emre despite a willingness to keep sitting near him.
Fond interest in Emre despite valuing him chiefly as material for writing.
Weary patience with Emre despite his talk going on to no real end.

items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 Emre의 말을 '갈매기 걸음'에 빗대 수첩에 적고 직원에게 보여 주며 웃음거리로 삼는다. 그러나 '꼭 조롱한 것은 아니었다'는 자기 정정이 이어지고, 뒤에서는 조용하고 따뜻한 대기실을 사양한 채 그의 곁에 남으며, 갈매기 문장이 적힌 쪽을 항구에 버린다. 떨어진 두 행동은 조롱하는 말투 아래 그의 고민을 진지하게 여기는 마음을 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 말투만 읽었고, C는 수첩에 쓴 일을 근거로 이유를 글감으로 돌렸지만 그 쪽을 버린 행동과 맞지 않으며, D는 지문의 'to no end'를 빌렸을 뿐 대기실을 사양한 선택을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: Yona ran the crew rewiring the old apartment block in Lisbon, and on my first morning he told me I held pliers the way a tourist holds a map. By April I kept a list of his sayings and read the best ones aloud to my flatmates, who asked for more. He timed my breaks. He called me "Mika the Apprentice" in front of the tenants. Once he made me strip and redo a junction box I knew was sound. His plan to finish the stairwell before the inspector came cost us three weeks of nights, and it worked; the inspector signed on a Friday, and the crew packed up as if someone had lost. I told my flatmates I would not miss him, which was true, more or less. The next spring a new boy joined the crew. On his first morning I watched him close a junction box, and then I handed him the screwdriver and told him to open it again.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Yona as conveyed in the text?
options: Lasting resentment of Yona despite relief that the long job has ended.
Unvoiced respect for Yona's standards despite a comic record of his gibes.
Real fondness for Yona despite a sense that he singled her out unfairly.
Mild tolerance of Yona despite expecting not to miss him very much.

items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 Yona의 비꼬는 말을 목록으로 만들어 친구들 앞에서 웃음거리로 읽고, 휴식 시간을 재거나 멀쩡한 배선함을 다시 하게 한 일을 불평처럼 나열한다. 중간의 '어느 정도는 사실이었다'는 망설이는 정정이 그 말을 누그러뜨리고, 마지막에 화자는 새로 들어온 소년에게 Yona가 자신에게 시켰던 것처럼 배선함을 다시 열게 한다. 그의 엄격한 기준을 그대로 물려주는 행동은 말로 하지 않은 존경을 보여 주므로 B가 정답이다. A는 불평의 말투만 읽었고, C는 이유를 부당하게 표적이 되었다는 감정으로 바꾸었으며, D는 'would not miss him'을 빌렸지만 마지막 행동을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: What is a reputation made of, if not of things nobody sees? For six years Ngozi rode Dewi's omnibus from the Marina to her shop, and for six years she called for her stop by rapping a brass thimble twice on the rail, a sound Dewi privately thought rather grand for a woman who paid the same fare as a fishmonger. All Lagos knew her for the coats she cut for merchants' weddings, and all Lagos supposed those coats had made her rich. In the wet season Dewi carried a torn jacket to her shop and was sent through to the back room to wait. Under a lamp lay a heap of garments no merchant would wear: patched shirts, a porter's trousers, a child's frock, each pinned with a name and no figure. On the bench sat a second thimble, worn so thin at the crown that the lamp showed through it. The next morning, when Ngozi lifted her hand, Dewi had already drawn up the horses.
items.question: In the text, the thimble most likely represents
options: the unseen labor on which the tailor's good name actually rests.
the tailor's way of claiming notice from those who serve her.
a passenger's bond with her driver that is strained and then mended.
the tool that guards a tailor's fingers through long hours of sewing.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 사물이 두 맥락에서 다른 의미를 띠고, 가장 강한 오답이 인물 관계로 읽은 그럴듯한 상징 해석이다
items.explanation: 골무는 처음에 Ngozi가 내릴 곳을 알리려고 난간을 두드리는 도구로 나오고, Dewi는 그 소리를 다소 거만하다고 여긴다. 그러나 뒷방에서 Dewi는 값 없이 이름만 붙은 가난한 이들의 옷 더미와 빛이 비칠 만큼 닳은 두 번째 골무를 본다. 다음 날 그가 그녀가 손을 들자마자 이미 마차를 세워 두는 변화는, 골무가 부유하다는 소문 아래 숨은 그녀의 무보수 노동을 가리키게 되었음을 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 앞 맥락의 인상만 반영했고, D는 문자적 기능이며, C는 Dewi의 생각 변화를 두 사람 관계의 손상과 회복으로 잘못 읽었다.

items.passage: When the minibus to Entoto is late, which is most mornings, the queue at the stop leans into the wind like a row of fence posts. Baraka, whose father owns our building, waits at the front with a plastic jug of water he never drinks. He has stood there since my mother's knee gave out. Each morning he hands her the jug at the corner, where the road turns steep, and walks on before she can find her purse. Each month the rent notice under our door comes a little later than the month before, and nobody in our flat remarks on it. My cousin, up from Durban for a week, watched all this once from the stop. That night, drying plates, she called Baraka the shim under our table, and my mother laughed and said our table had always stood perfectly level. In the morning, when I set down the bread, the table rocked.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the shim under our table” most nearly suggests
options: a small kindness the family could manage without if it had to
a quiet support that keeps the household steady without notice
a wedge the landlord's family uses to keep the tenants in check
a stopgap that disguises how unsteady the household has become
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 Baraka는 어머니의 무릎이 다친 뒤 매일 가파른 길모퉁이에서 물통을 건네고 값을 치를 틈도 주지 않으며, 집세 고지서는 매달 조금씩 늦어지지만 가족은 아무도 이를 말하지 않는다. 이 두 단서는 가족이 의식하지 못하는 사이 그가 집안을 받치고 있음을 보여 주므로 '탁자 밑 쐐기'는 눈에 띄지 않는 지지를 뜻하고 B가 정답이다. 어머니가 탁자는 늘 평평했다고 웃은 뒤 다음 날 탁자가 흔들리는 장면도 받침이 실제로 있었음을 뒷받침한다. A는 크기, C는 압박이라는 다른 속성으로 읽었고, D는 임시방편이라는 속성을 골랐지만 지문은 집안의 불안정을 감추는 것이 아니라 받쳐 주는 쪽을 보여 준다.

items.passage:
Reels arrive on Marlon's bicycle each Thursday,
tins strapped behind him like stacked moons.
He climbs the iron stairs to my booth
and stays to watch me thread the gate.
My husband ran this lamp for thirty years;
the owners still send lilies on his birthday
and a card that says the town is grateful.
No envelope has ever come with either.
Three nights a week I splice what breaks,
re-cut the sprockets, trim the scorched frames
so no one in the dark below can tell.
The audience applauds the actors.
Marlon applauds the leader running out.
I am the seam in a borrowed coat.
Downstairs the ushers sweep the aisles;
the owners count the house.
At midnight Marlon counts my coins for the bus,
slips one of his own into the pile,
and walks his bicycle beside me down the hill.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the seam in a borrowed coat” most nearly suggests
options: a hidden flaw she must keep the people below from ever noticing
a tie to her husband's post that she holds only for a time
unseen work that joins each showing while others take the credit
a weak point where the theater's business may soon come apart

items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 화자는 끊어진 필름을 잇고 타 버린 프레임을 다듬어 관객이 눈치채지 못하게 하지만, 박수는 배우에게 가고 소유주의 감사 카드에는 돈 봉투가 한 번도 없었다. 이 두 단서는 솔기가 상영을 이어 붙이면서도 인정받지 못하는 노동을 가리킴을 보여 주므로 C가 정답이다. 비유 뒤 Marlon이 화자의 동전에 자기 돈을 몰래 보태는 장면은 그 노동을 알아보는 사람이 한 명은 있음을 확인한다. A는 솔기를 감춰야 할 결점으로, B는 '빌린'을 남편 자리의 일시성으로, D는 터질 수 있는 약점으로 읽어 각각 다른 속성만 골랐다.

items.passage: Wet clay and kiln dust: the wharf studio smelled as always on the morning after the newspaper printed its photograph of their collapsed display at the harbor fair. Meera, the elder, had always checked each shelf twice before a show and each glaze recipe three times, and she had checked the fair stand too; the trestle had simply given way. Annika came in late with the paper folded under her arm and set it face down on the counter. All morning visitors drifted in, looked, and drifted out. Meera stayed at the wheel, and her manner toward them was ______. She greeted each by name and answered what was asked, offering nothing further, and when a child knocked a cup from the low shelf, she swept up the pieces before the mother could speak and told her, smiling, that it had been a second anyway.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: stiffly formal
carefully composed
warmly attentive
quietly apologetic
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 빈칸 뒤 정의가 없고 두 제약을 동시에 만족하는 표현만 정답이며, 오답이 모두 문법적으로 맞고 의미 영역이 같다
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Meera는 전시 전마다 선반과 유약 배합을 몇 번씩 확인하는 철저한 사람으로 그려져, 빈칸에는 스스로를 다잡는 통제된 태도가 어울린다. 빈칸 뒤에서 그녀는 손님을 이름으로 맞고 묻는 말에만 답하며, 컵이 깨지자 웃으며 어차피 B급품이었다고 넘긴다. 이름을 부르고 웃는 행동은 딱딱함과 맞지 않고, 더 말을 보태지 않는 행동은 적극적인 다정함과 맞지 않으므로 두 조건을 모두 만족하는 B가 정답이다. A는 절제만, C는 친절만 반영한 표현이고, D는 신문 사진이라는 사건의 수치심을 빌렸지만 그녀는 사과하지 않는다.

items.passage: Four hundred sheets an hour was the rule of the night shift, and Rukhsana kept to it as she kept to everything, counting under her breath and never stopping the press to talk. Her uncle had left his share in the shop to the two of us together, and a buyer from Bombay had written to offer for it. For a week I spoke of nothing else, and she inked the forme, pulled the lever, and set each sheet aside. At last, past midnight, I asked her plainly whether we ought to sell. Her answer was ______. She said that the price was a fair one. Then she counted the stack she had just pulled and began another, and in the morning I found the buyer's letter on my desk, its corners squared to the edge of the blotter, unsigned.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: briskly efficient
cautiously approving
guardedly noncommittal
politely dismissive

items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Rukhsana는 규칙대로 일하며 일을 멈추고 말하는 법이 없는 인물로 그려져, 그녀의 대답은 속을 드러내지 않는 쪽이어야 한다. 빈칸 뒤에서 그녀는 값이 공정하다고만 말하고 다시 일로 돌아가며, 다음 날 편지를 버리지도 서명하지도 않은 채 반듯하게 놓아 둔다. 찬성도 거절도 드러내지 않고 결정을 미루는 태도이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 앞의 작업 습관만 반영했고, B는 '공정하다'는 말만 보고 서명하지 않은 행동을 놓쳤으며, D는 편지를 정성껏 정리해 돌려준 행동과 정도가 맞지 않는다.

"Read it again," Akari said, the mayor's notice folding in her glove.
Each evening on the Riga platform I had watched Kalani, the town's only doctor,
copy such notices into three tongues, slowly,
testing every verb against the worn dictionary in her coat.
Tonight the train was late; the lamps hummed above the rails.
Akari set a finger on one line: her word for "closed"
had become "abandoned" on the sheet already pasted to the wall.
Kalani was ______ by the error.
She neither argued nor begged pardon.
She drew a pencil from her coat, struck the word on the posted sheet,
and wrote the smaller word above it, letter by letter,
while the arriving train swallowed whatever Akari said next.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

mildly amused
rather unconcerned

앞부분에서 Kalani는 매일 저녁 모든 동사를 사전과 대조할 만큼 번역의 정확성을 중시하는 인물이므로, 오류에 무심하거나 즐거워할 수 없다. 뒷부분에서 그녀는 따지지도 사과하지도 않고 연필로 한 글자씩 조용히 고쳐 쓰므로, 반응은 겉으로 드러나지 않는 동요여야 한다. 두 조건을 모두 만족하는 것은 D이다. A는 오류를 중히 여긴다는 점은 맞지만 드러난 수치심이라는 정도가 사과하지 않는 침착한 행동과 어긋나고, B와 C는 정확성에 대한 그녀의 꼼꼼함과 맞지 않는다.
